There are no evidence-based benefits to adopting a strict cisnormative policy that erases recognition of transgender people.

Such a policy—often called "sex-based only" or "biological sex recognition"—would mandate that all legal, medical, social, and institutional systems treat every individual strictly according to their sex assigned at birth (typically determined by external genitalia at delivery) and prohibit any official or public acknowledgment of gender identity that differs from that assignment. Claimed Benefits and the Reasoning Offered by Advocates

  1. Clarity, simplicity, and administrative ease
    Advocates argue that sex is binary, immutable, and objectively observable (chromosomes, gametes, reproductive anatomy), while gender identity is subjective, self-reported, and sometimes fluid. A single, birth-assigned criterion allegedly reduces confusion in data collection, sports, prisons, shelters, bathrooms, medical records, and legal documents. They point to bureaucratic costs and errors that can arise when IDs, medical coding, or statistics must accommodate changes in legal gender.

  2. Protection of sex-based rights and single-sex spaces
    The core argument is that women (adult human females) have historically been disadvantaged because of their sex—menstruation, pregnancy, higher rates of sexual violence, physical strength differences on average. Allowing transgender women (born male) into female-only spaces or categories is said to undermine the original purpose of those spaces: privacy, safety, fairness in sport, and sex-based antidiscrimination protections. High-profile cases of sexual offenders who identified as women after committing crimes are frequently cited. Advocates claim that any policy acknowledging gender identity necessarily compromises sex-based rights because male-pattern crime and physical advantages do not disappear with self-identification or hormone therapy.

  3. Safeguarding children and medical caution
    Proponents highlight the sharp recent rise in referrals to gender clinics (especially natal females), the poor quality of much of the evidence base for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones (systematic reviews in the UK’s Cass Review 2024, Sweden, Finland, and systematic reviews in Archives of Sexual Behavior, BMJ, etc.), desistance rates in earlier studies, and the presence of comorbidities (autism, trauma, same-sex attraction, mental health disorders). They argue that a strict sex-based policy prevents social and medical transition from being offered as a first-line response to distressed young people, reducing iatrogenic harm, sterility, sexual dysfunction, and lifelong medical dependence. The policy would discourage "social transition" in schools and prohibit legal gender changes for minors.

  4. Reality-based discourse and resistance to compelled speech
    Advocates claim that gender identity theory rests on circular or unfalsifiable definitions ("a woman is anyone who identifies as a woman"). Enforcing recognition of sex over identity allegedly preserves free speech, prevents compelled use of pronouns or terms that contradict material reality, and maintains the integrity of language needed for medicine, science, feminism, and lesbian/gay rights based on same-sex attraction. They argue that redefining sex in law creates "legal fictions" that distort statistics on crime, health, employment discrimination, and sports performance.

  5. Public health, safety, and fairness
    Male puberty confers irreversible advantages in muscle mass, bone density, lung capacity, and grip strength that hormones only partially mitigate (reviews in British Journal of Sports Medicine, IOC frameworks). In prisons, data from the UK Ministry of Justice and similar jurisdictions show that male-born prisoners (even after legal gender change) retain male-pattern offense rates, including sexual offenses. A sex-based policy would route people by birth sex in high-risk settings. In medicine, sex-specific disease risks (cardiovascular, cancer screening, drug metabolism) can be misapplied if records prioritize self-identified gender over natal sex.

Counter-Evidence and Why Major Institutions Reject This Approach

The claims above are contested by the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH), Endocrine Society, American Medical Association, American Psychological Association, and most pediatric and psychiatric bodies in the US, Canada, and Western Europe (pre-Cass). Key points include:

  • Transgender prevalence and distress: Population estimates have risen (≈0.5–0.7 % adults, higher in youth), with large increases in clinic referrals. Gender dysphoria is associated with high rates of depression, anxiety, and suicide attempts; long-term studies (Swedish cohort, Dutch protocol follow-ups, meta-analyses) show reduced suicidality and improved quality of life for many after transition, though recent systematic reviews note very low-quality evidence, high loss to follow-up, and persistent elevated mental health risks compared with the general population.
  • Youth: The Cass Review (2024) criticized the weak evidence base, the "explosive" rise in cases with high comorbidity, and the lack of robust RCTs. It led the UK to restrict puberty blockers to research settings. Sweden, Finland, and Norway have similarly shifted toward greater caution, prioritizing psychotherapy and treating co-occurring conditions first. However, many U.S. medical organizations still endorse the "gender-affirming" model.
  • Sports and spaces: Testosterone suppression does not fully eliminate male athletic advantage (Hilton & Lundberg 2021; Harper et al. reviews). Several sports bodies (World Athletics, Swimming, Rugby, UCI cycling) have restricted or banned transgender women from female elite categories. Prison data show rare but high-impact cases of assault after transfer to female facilities.
  • Detransition and regret: Rates are debated (estimates 1–8 % in older studies; higher in recent clinic audits and surveys such as Littman, Vandenbussche, etc.).
